name: Sam Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an energy lawyer at Greenhalgh Reid, about sixty lawyers, and my clients are community solar co-ops and small councils trying to get wind and solar projects onto the grid. A normal day is negotiating grid connection contracts, which are three hundred pages of who pays if a cable fails, plus calls with volunteer boards who are retired teachers running a solar farm. I love those boards. What wears me out is the grid operator taking eight months to answer one email.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned the contracts are three hundred pages. How do you get through them?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: With AI, every day. I've built my own set of prompts that pull out every payment clause and every risk on liability, and I check the summary against the contract, which takes an hour instead of a day. I'm twenty-seven, I live with my partner Jonah, who's a sound engineer for live gigs, and I've got about fourteen months saved plus a small index fund. I'm the person juniors come to when the AI tool does something odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I've bet a lot of my working style on these tools getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful but not magic, which is what I already tell people. At work I'd keep running the lunchtime sessions where I show associates how to check an AI summary against the source.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm a bit ahead of the curve and that's all. My job's safe, my pay stays good, and the co-ops keep needing lawyers who understand the grid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using my prompts every day and keep doing the lunchtime sessions. I'd keep putting £500 a month into the index fund and maybe take the energy regulation course I've been putting off. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little let down, like a band you loved putting out a dull album.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've bet your working style on these tools. Is that a risk in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. If AI stalls, I've only lost the hours I spent writing prompts, and I'd still read a three-hundred-page grid contract faster than the partner who laughed at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what still bothers you about the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grid queue. Some of my co-ops have waited four years for a connection, and no AI plateau or boom fixes a shortage of cables and engineers. That's a hands-on problem and a political one.

say: The tools are **useful but not magic**, as I already tell people.
I'd keep teaching **lunchtime sessions** on checking AI summaries against sources.
think: I'm a bit **ahead of the curve**, and that's all it means.
My job, **pay** and co-op clients stay secure.
do: Keep using my **own prompts** daily on grid contracts.
Put **£500 a month** into the index fund.
Take the **energy regulation course** I've delayed.
S0.quote: If AI stalls, I've only lost the hours I spent writing prompts, and I'd still read a three-hundred-page grid contract faster than the partner who laughed at me.
fieldNote: He's **secure** and adaptive, so a plateau costs him almost nothing.
His real frustration is the **grid queue**, a physical and political problem.
He's the office **AI helper**, which gives him status he'd keep either way.

steps.text: Keep running lunchtime sessions on checking AI contract summaries
Keep advising solar co-ops on grid connection contracts
Put £500 a month into the index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I think is most likely. Writing and checking are exactly what I already hand to AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains have to be shared. If the firm bills the same and does it with half the associates, the partners pocket the difference, and I'd say that out loud at the associates' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do well. I'd be the one running the AI workflows, so I'd probably get promoted faster. But the trainees I teach at lunch would be the ones not hired next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch the partners a fixed-fee grid contract review for co-ops, done with AI and checked by me, within three months. I'd ask for a seat on the firm's tech committee. And I'd join the campaign group pushing for a four-day week in law firms, because that's where the saved time should go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Good for me, bad for the people around me, and I'm not sure I like being on the winning side of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do well. Who loses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainees. Every hour AI saves me at the firm should go to the co-op or to a shorter week, not into a partner's bonus. If it doesn't, the trainee seats go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a trainee who asks if they should still become a lawyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a trainee to come anyway but to learn energy or housing, where the human fights are, not routine contract review. And to join a union early, even if lawyers think unions are for other people.

say: The **time AI saves** should be shared, not pocketed by partners.
Law firms should move to a **four-day week** with the gains.
think: I'd likely be **promoted faster** for running the AI work.
The **trainees** I teach at lunch would not be hired.
do: Pitch a **fixed-fee review** for co-ops within three months.
Ask for a seat on the firm's **tech committee**.
Join the **four-day week** campaign for law firms.
feel: **Uneasy** about being on the winning side.
Good for himself, **guilty** about the people around him.
S1.quote: Every hour AI saves me at the firm should go to the co-op or to a shorter week, not into a partner's bonus.
fieldNote: He's an **early adopter** with a progressive conscience, and the two pull against each other.
His action is both **personal gain** and campaigning for shared gains.
He'd steer trainees to **contested areas** like energy and housing.

steps.text: Pitch partners a fixed-fee AI grid contract review for co-ops
Ask for a seat on the firm's tech committee
Join the campaign for a four-day week in law firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is brutal. I'd be twenty-nine and most of my job would be done by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need public ownership of the big AI systems, or at least a public stake. I'd write it, post it and say it at work, because if the gains go to five companies, everyone else is a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my desk job as a contract lawyer is gone. Robots arriving three years later is irrelevant to me, because I don't touch anything but a keyboard. The part that might survive is sitting with a co-op board and helping them decide, and that's maybe a fifth of my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd talk to the co-op network about becoming their in-house lawyer and organiser, on lower pay. I'd cut my fund contributions and hold six more months of cash. And I'd join whatever union for professionals formed, because there'd be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I lose the job as it is, but I've got money and a direction, so it doesn't keep me up yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a fifth of your week survives. Is that enough to live on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on my current pay, no. It'd be maybe £35,000 instead of £70,000. I could live on it with no kids and a cushion, but I'd stop pretending I'm a high earner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Jonah's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Jonah mixes live sound at gigs, and in a two-year AGI world his job, the one everybody called unstable, becomes the steadier one in our flat. He'd have till 2031 before robots catch up.

say: The big AI systems need **public ownership** or a public stake.
If the gains go to **five companies**, everyone else is just a customer.
think: My **desk job** as a contract lawyer is gone within two years.
Only the **co-op board** work survives, about a fifth of my week.
Later **robots** don't help me; I only touch a keyboard.
do: Ask the **co-op network** to hire me as lawyer and organiser on lower pay.
Stop fund contributions and hold **six more months** of cash.
feel: **Anxious**, but money and a direction keep sleep intact for now.
S2.quote: My partner Jonah mixes live sound at gigs, and in a two-year AGI world his job, the one everybody called unstable, becomes the steadier one in our flat.
fieldNote: He expects to lose **most of his role** but keeps control through savings and a plan.
His household hedge is **Jonah's hands-on job**, which gets three more years.
His answer is **structural**: public ownership and a union, not just personal moves.

steps.text: Ask the co-op network to hire him as in-house lawyer and organiser
Stop index fund payments and build six more months of cash
Join a new union for lawyers and other professionals
Write and campaign for a public stake in big AI systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to build something rather than run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same about public ownership, but I'd add that five years is enough time for the law society to retrain people properly if it starts now. I'd volunteer to help design that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd use the time to set up a not-for-profit legal clinic for community energy groups, staffed by a few lawyers and a lot of AI. When AGI arrives the clinic just gets cheaper, not useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the clinic as a side project in year one, two evenings a week, with two other associates. By year three I'd go part-time at the firm. I'd put about £15,000 of savings into setting it up, which I can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited too. Five years feels like a sprint I can actually run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the clinic gets cheaper, not useless. Why wouldn't AGI replace it too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could write the documents, sure. But a co-op board of retired teachers doesn't want a chatbot to sign off a solar farm; they want someone they can look in the eye and blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk if the clinic fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lose fifteen grand and some evenings, and I go back to a firm that by then might not want me. That's the real risk, being out of the firm world just as it shrinks.

I'd volunteer to help **design retraining** for lawyers.

steps.text: Start a not-for-profit energy legal clinic two evenings a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole second career's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty if we use it, and I'd keep pushing for public ownership and a shorter working week. I'd be the annoying optimist in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I can build the clinic slowly, keep the firm salary longer, and maybe retrain in energy policy so I can work for a council or the grid regulator. I'd have options most people don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time master's in energy policy over two years. I'd start the clinic in year three, not year one. I'd keep £500 a month going into the fund and use AI more and more in the firm work so I know its limits when it gets big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own path feels fine, but I'd be watching friends in other desk jobs who aren't planning at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Tom in insurance thinks ten years means never, and I can already see him at forty learning to code for a job that won't exist. A couple of friends in marketing are the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a decade make you feel safer, or just later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Later, honestly. The end point is the same. I'd just rather meet the end point at thirty-seven with a clinic and a policy degree than at twenty-nine with a contract and a laptop.

I'd keep pushing for **public ownership** and a shorter working week.
think: Ten years lets me keep the **firm salary** and build slowly.
A move into **energy policy** at a council or the regulator is open to me.

Start the **clinic** in year three instead of year one.

feel: **Uneasy** for friends in desk jobs who aren't planning.

fieldNote: He sees **ten years** as 'later, not safer', but feels in control.
His unease is mostly about **friends** with no plan.
He keeps **investing** steadily, which fits his strong cushion.

steps.text: Do a part-time master's in energy policy over two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even with savings and Jonah's work, I'd be rebuilding at twenty-nine with no time. What would help is a public stake in the AI systems, so the gains pay for retraining, and a union for professionals that exists before we need it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether I trust myself to be the one who stays. Everyone who's good with the tools thinks they'll be fine, and the tools don't care how good I am with them.

headlineQuote: Everyone who's good with the tools thinks they'll be fine, and the tools don't care how good I am with them.
portrait: A 27-year-old **energy lawyer** advising community solar co-ops and councils on grid contracts.
He uses AI **every day**, with his own prompts, and teaches colleagues at lunch.
He lives with Jonah, a **live sound engineer**, with fourteen months saved and an index fund.
Calm in AI Plateau, he stays **anxious but planning** under fast AGI, eyeing a co-op role.
He blames **concentrated ownership** of AI and wants public stakes, unions and a shorter week.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be rebuilding at twenty-nine with no time.
whatWouldHelp: A **public stake** in AI systems so the gains pay for retraining.
A **professionals' union** set up before it's needed.
